ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The figure shows a capacitively coupled NPN common-emitter amplifier circuit. The upper power supply is 12 V; the collector is connected to 12 V through a 3 kΩ resistor; the base is biased by voltage division of 100 kΩ and 20 kΩ, and receives the input vi(t) through the 100 nF coupling capacitor on the left side; the emitter is grounded through 900 Ω, and has a 10 μF capacitor bypass; the output is taken from the collector through the 100 nF coupling capacitor on the right side, labeled vo(t). Reasoning: The input signal vi(t)=A cos(20t)+B sin(10^6 t) can be analyzed separately for the two frequency components. For the low-frequency component of ω=20 rad/s, the capacitive reactance of the 100 nF coupling capacitor is about 1/(20·100 nF)=500 kΩ, much larger than the input and output related resistances of the amplifier, so this low-frequency component is basically blocked by the coupling capacitor, and its contribution to the output can be ignored. For the high-frequency component of ω=10^6 rad/s, the capacitive reactance of the 100 nF coupling capacitor is about 10 Ω, and the capacitive reactance of the 10 μF emitter bypass capacitor is about 0.1 Ω, both of which can be approximately regarded as short circuits, so the emitter is AC ground, and the circuit works as a common-emitter amplifier. The small-signal voltage gain is approximately Av≈-βRC/hie=-150·(3 kΩ)/(3 kΩ)=-150. Therefore only the high-frequency term is effectively amplified and inverted, giving vo(t)≈-150B sin(10^6 t).

The small-signal voltage gain is approximately Av≈-βRC/hie=-150·(3 kΩ)/(3 kΩ)=-150. Therefore only the high-frequency term is effectively amplified and inverted, giving vo(t)≈-150B sin(10^6 t).
